{{Short description|Hungarian mathematician}}

'''Stefánia Szilárd''' was a Hungarian-Soviet mathematician. She and her husband, [[Ervin Bauer]], emigrated to the USSR in 1925 and were killed during the [[Great Purge]] a decade later. [[Karl Szilárd]], also a mathematician, was her younger brother (the two had no relation to [[Leo Szilard]]).<ref name='Zusmanovich' />

Szilárd was born in 1898 in [[Győr]] (then Austria-Hungary). She graduated from the [[Eötvös Loránd University|Budapest University]]'s Faculty of Physics and Mathematics in 1919,<ref name='bauer' /> the same year marrying [[Ervin Bauer]], a noted physician and biologist, and a staunch supporter of the short-lived [[Hungarian Soviet Republic]]. After the fall of the Republic in 1919, and the ensuing [[White Terror (Hungary)|White Terror]], the couple fled the country and lived, under hardship conditions, in Göttingen, Prague, and Berlin.<ref name='Zusmanovich' />

After an invitation to Ervin Bauer by [[Nikolai Semashko (medicine)|Nikolai Semashko]], the Russian Commissar of Public Health of that time, they settled in 1925 in Moscow, moving to Leningrad in 1933.<ref name='bauer' /><ref name='Zusmanovich' /> Stefánia's younger brother, [[Karl Szilárd]], followed in 1934.<ref name='bauer'>{{Cite journal |last=Bauer |first=Svetlana M. |date=2024 |title=Life and fate of Ervin Bauer (1890–1938), the eminent scholar and foundational theoretical biologist |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0303264724000765 |journal=BioSystems |volume=238 |article-number=105191 |doi=10.1016/j.biosystems.2024.105191 |pmid=38508229 |bibcode=2024BiSys.23805191B |issn=0303-2647|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In Moscow the Bauers socialized with other Hungarian emigres, including [[Máté Zalka]], [[Béla Illés (writer)|Béla Illés]], and [[Antal Hidas]].<ref name='bauer' />

Stefánia became a member of the communist party, and worked, together with her husband, at the Leningrad branch of the [[Institute of Experimental Medicine]]. According to her contemporaries, she was an able mathematician, but her life apparently was dominated by the life and deeds of her husband, whom she helped in his work in theoretical biology. During her life, she published only two short papers – one in Hungarian in 1917 on [[number theory]], and another one in 1934 (written in German and published in ''[[Matematicheskii Sbornik]]'')<ref name='bauer' /> on [[complex analysis]].<ref name='Zusmanovich' />

The couple was arrested in August 1937 and shot in January 1938.<ref name='bauer' /> They are buried in [[Levashovo Memorial Cemetery]].<ref name='bauer' /> They were both [[Rehabilitation (Soviet)|rehabilitated]] in 1956.<ref name='bauer' />

==Family==
Ervin and Stefánia had three children: Mikhail (born in 1924), Sophia (born in 1928, died of pneumonia at the age of four), and Karl (born in 1934).<ref name='bauer' /> After their deaths, their two surviving children were separated, given different family names, and sent to orphanages.<ref name='Zusmanovich'>Pasha Zusmanovich, [https://scholarship.claremont.edu/jhm/vol14/iss1/8 "Mathematicians Going East,"] Journal of Humanistic Mathematics, Volume 14 Issue
1 (January 2024), pages 114-167. DOI: 10.5642/jhummath.EGCM7534. Pages 118-119.</ref> As an adult Mikhail Bauer served in a [[labor army]] and was sent to [[Barnaul]] to work in an engineering plant before returning to Leningrad in 1956. He published a memoir in 2003.<ref name='bauer' />
